title: The turning
hook: the Mevlevi order's turning ceremony, one hand up, one hand down

segments.voice: Yesterday, hal, a state of the heart: moods that come to teach and then leave, and days that take their turns. Your line: every state is a guest.

The picture travels far beyond Turkey, on posters, postcards and screens: men in tall honey-colored felt hats and long white skirts, turning, turning, skirts flaring out like bells, heads tilted, eyes half closed. People call them whirling dervishes. It looks like a dance. The people who do it call it something else, and their word is about the ears, not the feet.
screen: `TALL HATS, WHITE SKIRTS.` → `TURNING, EYES HALF CLOSED.` → `A WORD ABOUT THE EARS.`

segments.voice: The word is sama'. It means listening, from the same root as as-Sami', the All-Hearing, one of the names of God. For Sufis, sama' means listening to music, poetry or the Qur'an with the heart until you're moved by it. The Mevlevi order, named for Rumi, Mawlana, turned that listening into a ceremony. Tradition says Rumi himself would sometimes turn in ecstasy, and people tell a story that it began when he heard goldbeaters hammering in the Konya bazaar. The formal ceremony was shaped after his death, by his son and later generations. Everything in it carries meaning. The tall hat is said to stand for the tombstone of the ego. The white skirt, the shroud. The black cloak they take off at the start, the grave left behind. The music: the ney, the reed flute, and a drum. And the arms: right palm up to the sky, left palm down to the earth. As the Mevlevis explain it, what comes from God is received through the right hand and passed on to the world through the left. The turner keeps nothing. Receive, give. They turn around their own hearts, and they turn together, like planets. In modern Turkey the orders were closed, and for decades the ceremony survived mostly as a cultural performance. UNESCO now lists it as part of humanity's cultural heritage. And Muslims hold different views on music in worship: some scholars allow musical sama', and others do not accept it at all. Those differences come up again soon.
screen: `SAMA' — LISTENING.` · `HAT, SHROUD, CLOAK.` · `RIGHT HAND UP, LEFT HAND DOWN.` · `NOT ALL MUSLIMS ACCEPT IT.` · then, large: `RECEIVE, GIVE.`

segments.voice: If you can stand safely, lift your right hand a little, palm up, let your left hang low, palm down, soften your eyes, and turn slowly once, all the way round, feeling the floor under your feet; then stand still and breathe. If you can't stand, just turn your palms, one up, one down, and sit with them. Picture receiving through one and giving through the other.
Sama'. Listening with the heart; for the Mevlevis, the turning ceremony, one hand up, one hand down. Today's word.
Your line: receive, give. One palm to the sky, one to the earth. See you tomorrow.

chat.says: Why do the whirling dervishes turn with one palm up and one palm down?
options: They receive from God through the raised hand and pass it to the world through the lower one.
It keeps them balanced while spinning; the hands themselves don't carry any meaning.
The raised hand asks God for blessing, and the lower one keeps it safe for themselves.
